name: Interview behavioural questions, set 7
description: Spoken behavioural questions with model answers and rubrics: data that persuaded, a choice to stop, help at a cost, testing the fit, "are you sure", a lost contest, quiet in meetings and a CV claim. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: the mind changed with data.

widget.prompt: Tell me about a time you changed someone's mind with data.
widget.model: I volunteered at the student food bank, which opened on Friday afternoons. The coordinator was sure Friday was best, because that was when students ran short before the weekend. I thought weekday evenings might reach more people, but my opinion alone would not move her. So for four weeks I logged every visit by hour and asked each visitor one question: when could you come? Of the 212 people I asked, 61 per cent said Friday afternoons clashed with labs or shifts. I put it on one bar chart, the times we opened against the times people asked for, and showed it at the committee meeting in under five minutes. The coordinator asked how I had chosen whom to ask, which was fair, so I showed her the log. We added a Tuesday evening session as a trial. The next term it had 140 visits, and Friday visits held steady. Now she asks for a log before any change.

rubric.text: Names the claim you disputed and whose mind you set out to change
The data you gathered, with how much and how
The single chart or number that carried the case, stated
The decision that followed, with its result as a number
Shows you took the other person's objection seriously
Under 300 words, told in order, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: The interviewer wants evidence chosen to answer a question, not data used as decoration. Name the claim, say how you gathered the numbers and give the one figure that moved the decision. Ending on the result shows the change was worth making.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: the work you chose to stop.

widget.prompt: Describe a time you chose to stop working on something.
widget.model: In my second-year summer I spent six weeks in a materials lab, writing software to find cracks in microscope images. By week three my classifier found 70 per cent of cracks, and I wanted 90. I spent another eight days on new features and reached 73. Then I checked what the lab did with the output. A technician reviewed every flagged image by hand anyway, so the tool's value was in sorting images, not in final answers. I wrote down what I had sunk, about eleven days, and asked what the next eight days would buy. The answer was perhaps three more points that no one would use. I told my supervisor I wanted to stop, with those numbers, and she agreed. I spent the last three weeks on a tool that sorted images by how likely they were to show a crack. It cut the technician's review from two days a week to about half a day. I now ask early who uses the output, and how.

rubric.text: Names what you stopped and what you had already put into it, in time or effort
The evidence that more work would not pay, with a number
Compares the next effort with its gain, so the sunk cost does not decide
Says whom you told and how they responded
What the freed time went to, with its result
Under 300 words, told in order, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: This question tests whether you can let go of a sunk cost. Show the evidence that more effort would not pay, and weigh the next days against what they would buy. Then say what the time went to, so stopping reads as a choice.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: help that cost you something.

widget.prompt: Tell me about a time you helped someone succeed at a cost to yourself.
widget.model: In my second year a flatmate on my programming module missed three weeks through illness. Our individual coursework was due in ten days, and she had not started. I offered two evenings a week to go through the material with her. I set one rule: I would explain, but I would not write any of her code. Over those ten days I gave her about twelve hours. That time came from my own economics essay, which I finished in a rush and which got 58, against the high sixties I usually score. I chose it because twelve hours could decide whether she passed the module, while my essay counted for five per cent of my year. She passed the coursework with 64 and went on to the second-year course. I lost a few marks I would like back. Next time I would offer help earlier, so it does not crowd out my own deadline.

rubric.text: States what the help was and whom it was for, early
The cost to you in hours or marks, as a number
The reason you chose it, weighing your cost against their gain
What happened to the other person, as an outcome
A rule that kept the help fair, such as not doing their work
What you would do differently next time

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: The interviewer is looking for judgement, not sacrifice for its own sake. Put a number on the cost and say why it was worth paying against what the other person gained. A rule that kept the help honest shows you thought about fairness too.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: how you tested the fit.

widget.prompt: What have you done to find out whether you would like this work?
widget.model: I tried two things, each meant to test a different part of the job. First, I played in the university trading society's weekly market-making games for a whole term, twelve sessions. I wanted to know whether I enjoy deciding fast with incomplete information. I did: my sizing improved once I kept a log of each game, and I looked forward to those evenings more than anything else that term. Second, I spent a week shadowing a family friend who works in risk at a bank, to see the slower side of the work. That showed me how much of the job is checking other people's numbers and explaining them, which I found more interesting than I expected. The surprise was how much the desk talked. I had pictured people working alone at screens, but most decisions were made in short conversations. That is part of why I want a role where I trade and explain, not only build models.

rubric.text: Two things you actually did, each named with its length or size
What each one told you about the work, stated separately
One thing that surprised you, said plainly
Links what you learned to the role you are applying for
Shows you kept a record or measured something, not only impressions
Under 300 words, told in order, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: This question asks for evidence, not enthusiasm. Name what you tried and what each showed you, including a surprise, which proves you looked closely. Tying it to the role answers why you want this job.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: when asked if you are sure.

widget.prompt: You give an answer you believe, and I say: are you sure? Show me what you do next, out loud. You have two minutes.
widget.model: First, I would neither defend the answer nor drop it just because you asked. Say my answer was that a fair die takes six rolls on average to show a six. I would say: let me check it a second way. My first route was the mean of a geometric distribution, one over the chance, so one over a sixth. The second route is a recursion. Call the expected number of rolls E. I roll once; with chance one sixth I am done, and with chance five sixths I am back where I started. So E equals 1 plus five sixths of E. That gives one sixth of E equals 1, so E is 6. Two routes that share no steps agree, so I keep the answer and say so: yes, I am sure, and here is why. If the second route had disagreed, I would say which step I distrust, redo that step, and give the corrected number.

rubric.text: Neither keeps nor drops the answer before checking it
Checks by a second route that does not repeat the first
Says each step of the check aloud, with its numbers
Keeps or changes the answer and gives the reason
Says what you would do if the two routes disagreed
Short enough for two minutes, with the check stated step by step

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: The interviewer is testing calm under doubt, not the arithmetic. A second route that shares no steps with the first is the strongest check you can say aloud. Then commit: keep or change the answer, and say why.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: a contest you lost.

widget.prompt: You have thirty seconds to prepare and two minutes to answer. Describe a time you competed and lost.
widget.model: In my second year my partner and I reached the final of the university badminton doubles. We lost in three games, and the last one went 21 to 19. Afterwards I watched the club's video of the match and counted how we lost points. We lost 14 points on our own serve, almost all from short serves that floated too high and were attacked. In practice I had always served to the same spot, because it felt safe. So the next term I changed how I trained. Every session began with fifty short serves to three different targets, and my partner marked whether each one could be attacked. In six weeks the share that could be attacked fell from about one in four to one in ten. We reached the final again the next year and won it. I still count my serves, because the loss showed me that what felt safe in practice was what lost us the match.

rubric.text: Names the contest and the result in the first sentence or two
States the margin of the loss as a number
Finds a cause from evidence, such as a count or a recording
What you changed in practice, specifically and with a measure
The result of the change, as a number or an outcome
Short enough for two minutes, told in order

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A recorded answer gives you no follow-up questions, so state the margin and the cause yourself. Show the evidence you used to find what went wrong. Then describe the change in practice and how you measured it.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: feedback that you are quiet.

widget.prompt: Halfway through an internship your manager says your work is fine but you are quiet in meetings. What do you do in the next two weeks?
widget.model: First I would thank my manager and ask one question: which meetings matter most, and what would good look like there? Say she names the Monday desk meeting. Then I would make three dated changes. This week, before Monday, I would prepare one point from my own work, a number and what it means, and say it in the first ten minutes. By Wednesday I would ask a senior analyst whether I could present my project's results at Friday's review, five minutes with one chart. In week two I would ask one question in each meeting about something I did not understand. To check it worked, I would keep a short log: meetings attended, points made, questions asked. At the end of the two weeks I would book fifteen minutes with my manager, show her the log and ask whether it matches what she has seen. If it does not, I would ask her what to try next.

rubric.text: Asks the manager which meetings matter and what good looks like
Three actions, each with a day or week attached
Each action is something said or shown in a meeting, not only preparation
A way to check the change, such as a log or a count
A follow-up meeting with the manager at the end of the two weeks
Under 300 words, told in order, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: Return offers depend on being seen to improve, so treat the feedback as a short project. Make each action dated and visible, and keep a record you can show. Closing the loop with the manager turns the plan into evidence.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: proficient in Python, with evidence.

widget.prompt: Your CV says "proficient in Python". Tell me what that means, with evidence.
widget.model: It means I can design, build and test a working program in Python on my own. The best evidence is a tool I wrote for my department's teaching office. It assigns 300 students to tutorial groups, respecting their timetables and a cap of twelve per group. It is about 900 lines in six modules, with 60 unit tests that run on every change. The first version took three weeks. The office used it for two terms, and it cut the job from two days of spreadsheet work to under an hour. Along the way I learned to profile code. One loop over every pair of students took most of the run time, and replacing it with a lookup by timetable slot made the program forty times faster. What I cannot yet do well is write concurrent code. I have read about it, but I have not built anything that runs several tasks at once and been sure it was correct.

rubric.text: Defines proficient in one sentence, as what you can do
One program of your own, with its size and its purpose
Evidence it worked: who used it, its tests or a measured result
One specific thing you cannot yet do in the language
One technical problem you solved in it, with a number
No list of libraries or tools offered as evidence

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A CV word is only as good as the evidence behind it. Describe one program by size, purpose and result, and one problem you solved inside it. Naming a real gap makes the rest of the claim easier to believe.
